claims.text: Strength in multi-component concentrated alloys is primarily governed by local chemical short-range order and the associated spatial fluctuations in planar shear-fault energy.
Local chemical order and fault-energy fluctuations govern deformation behavior by changing dislocation pathways, faulting, and twinning.
Heat treatment can promote L12-type short-range order relative to the predominantly L11 state of homogenized CrCoNi.
Enhanced local chemical order makes the dislocation energy landscape more rugged and raises activation barriers for dislocation motion.
Enhanced short-range order increases resistance to dislocation motion through nanoscale pinning or segment detrapping.
Nanoclusters with modified local short-range order produce spatial fluctuations in the local shear-fault-energy landscape.
Local regions of high shear-fault energy act as dislocation-pinning regions.
Fault-energy fluctuations produce characteristically wavy dislocation configurations.
Changing short-range order modifies slip pathways and dislocation patterns.
Increasing short-range order reduces faulting tendencies and can modify twinning or deformation-induced structural transformation.
A heat-treated alloy with promoted L12 order will have a statistically significant increase in yield strength relative to the homogenized baseline.
A heat-treated alloy with promoted L12 order will have a statistically significant increase in ultimate tensile strength relative to the homogenized baseline.
The heat-treated L12-promoted state will exhibit more pronounced dislocation pinning and altered slip paths than the homogenized state.
The homogenized, more random or L11-dominated baseline has lower yield strength and more conventional dislocation motion without enhanced pinning.
The proposed mechanism should operate at ambient or cryogenic temperatures in metastable concentrated alloys susceptible to local chemical fluctuations.
The effect may diminish in fully equilibrated alloys or alloys lacking significant local chemical fluctuations.
Electron nanodiffraction assisted by atom-probe tomography can characterize L11- and L12-type short-range order in CrCoNi.
Holding composition constant while varying only heat treatment provides a controlled comparison for testing the proposed SRO mechanism.
